In this large mono-institutional cohort of pediatric PTCs, tumor tissue samples have been analyzed for point mutations and fusions. Overall, molecular alterations were detected in 131 out of 163 PTCs (80%). Fusion-driven PTCs showed more aggressive clinico-pathological features compared to mutation-driven and wild-type cases. These results highlight the importance of testing pediatric PTCs for gene rearrangement in routine characterization of tumors. Abstract Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) presents distinct clinico-pathological and molecular differences in children compared with adult patients. Whether the presence of rearrangements or point mutations is associated with aggressive PTC clinical presentation is still controversial. In this study, PTCs diagnosed in patients aged less than 18 years were retrospectively searched from the institutional archive and tumor tissue was tested for point mutations in BRAF and RAS genes and for rearrangements in RET, NTRK1, NTRK3, ALK, PPARG, BRAF and THADA. A total of 163 PTCs were analyzed. Point mutations were found in 83 (51%) and gene fusions in 48 cases (30%). The most frequent alteration was the BRAFV600E mutation (36.8%), followed by NTRK3 fusion (11%), NRAS mutation (10.4%) and RET fusion (10.4%). Fusion-driven PTCs showed more frequently infiltrative growth, larger tumors, extrathyroidal extension and N1b disease. PTCs showing solid growth pattern were significantly enriched in gene fusions. This is one of the largest cohorts of pediatric PTCs. Fusion-driven tumors most frequently show aggressive pathological features; the search for rearrangements, especially in tumors with solid areas, could improve the characterization of pediatric PTCs and offer possible therapeutic options. Introduction Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common malignancy of the endocrine system. When occurring in pediatric age, PTC presents different clinico-pathological characteristics compared with PTC in adult patients [1]. In pediatric patients, PTC at presentation most frequently shows pathological features of aggressiveness, including lymph node metastases, extrathyroidal extension and distant metastases [2]. On the other hand, even in the presence of these characteristics that typically indicate poorer prognosis in adults, PTC pediatric patients generally have a favorable clinical outcome and an excellent survival [1,3,4]. The histology of PTC in children could also differ from that generally observed in adults: rare variants, such as the diffuse sclerosing variant, can represent a common finding in pediatric PTC cohorts [5]. According to the American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines for pediatric nodules and differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), patients aged ≤18 years should be included in the pediatric age group. It is not clear whether further age subgroups (i.e., less than 10–15-year-old children) with different clinico-pathological characteristics could be identified [1]. From a molecular point of view, gene fusions acting as driver events in PTC tumorigenesis have shown to be more frequent in children than in adults, where the most frequent alterations involve point mutations in BRAF and RAS genes [1,6]. However, studies reveal a poor level of agreement on the reported frequencies of genetic alterations in pediatric thyroid tumors. For instance, over the last 10 years, BRAF mutations in pediatric PTC have been reported in frequencies ranging from 9 to 50% of patients [7,8,9,10,11,12]. TERT promoter mutations are associated with older age and, accordingly, their occurrence in pediatric PTCs is rare [12,13,14,15]. In a series of 27 PTCs in children, Prasad and colleagues found significant clinico-pathological differences between BRAF-driven and fusion-driven PTCs. In particular, fusion-positive PTCs more frequently showed larger size, infiltration of thyroid parenchyma, and lymphatic invasion [16]. If confirmed on a larger series, these results highlight the importance of analyzing not only classical point mutations, but also gene fusions in pediatric patients, even in the diagnostic setting. In the light of the recent approval of drugs specifically targeting rearranged genes, testing for gene fusions is emerging as an essential part of routine molecular pathology activity. In this retrospective cohort study, a consecutive series of PTC patients aged less than 18 years was tested for the presence of molecular alterations, including the most frequent point mutations and rearrangements. Clinico-pathological features of PTC were correlated to the type of molecular alteration. 2. fetched_contents.text: Mutational Analysis in Pediatric Thyroid Cancer and Correlations with Age, Ethnicity, and Clinical Presentation Abstract Background: Well-differentiated thyroid cancer (WDTC) incidence in pediatrics is rising, most being papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). The objective of the study was to assess the prevalence of different mutations in pediatric WDTC and correlate the genotype with the clinical phenotype. Methods: This is a single-center retrospective study. Thyroid tissue blocks from 42 consecutive pediatric WDTC patients who underwent thyroidectomy between 2001 and 2013 were analyzed at Quest Diagnostics for BRAFV600E, RAS mutations (N,K,H), and RET/PTC and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangements, using validated molecular methods. Thyroid carcinomas included PTC, follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC), and follicular variant of PTC (FVPTC). Results: Thirty-nine samples (29 females) were genotyped. The mean age at diagnosis was 14.7 years (range 7.9–18.4 years), and most were Hispanic (56.4%) or Caucasian (35.9%). The mean follow-up period was 2.9 years. Mutations were noted in 21/39 (53.8%), with both BRAFV600E (n = 9), and RET/PTC (n = 6) detected only in PTC. Mutations were detected in 2/5 FTC (PAX8/PPARγ and NRAS) and 3/6 FVPTC cases (PAX8/PPARγ). Of 28 PTC patients, 57.1% had mutations: 32.1% with BRAFV600E, 21.4% with RET/PTC, and 3.6% with NRAS. Of patients with BRAFV600E, 77.8% were Hispanic and 88.9% were >15 years, while all RET/PTC-positive patients were ≤15 years (p = 0.003). Tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis at diagnosis (or soon after 131I ablation) did not vary significantly based on the mutation. Conclusions: BRAFV600E was the most common mutation, especially in older and Hispanic adolescents. A larger, ethnically diverse pediatric cohort followed long term will enable the genotypic variability, clinical presentation, and response to therapy to be better assessed. Introduction Thyroid cancer represents the third most common pediatric solid tumor and the most common endocrine malignancy (1). The incidence of thyroid cancer in the United States has been rising in both adults and pediatric patients. Based on the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, the average age-adjusted annual incidence for thyroid cancer in children 0–20 years old, from 2008 to 2011, was 0.886 per 100,000 persons (2). Pediatric thyroid carcinoma and especially papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) has a more favorable course compared with adults, with a disease-specific mortality of <2% (3). However, at the time of diagnosis, pediatric patients often present with more advanced disease, and they frequently suffer from persistent or recurrent disease due to metastatic lymph nodes or lung metastases (3). The prevalence of different mutations in adult thyroid cancer has been presented in various reports. The most common genetic alteration is BRAF (29–83%) with an overall prevalence of ∼44% (4–6). The prevalence of RET/PTC rearrangements in adults has been estimated to be ∼35% (7). Point mutations in HRAS, KRAS, and NRAS are less frequent in PTC, with an overall frequency of 10–20% (8), whereas a higher prevalence (40–50%) has been reported in follicular carcinomas (9,10). Finally, PAX8/PPARγ rearrangements are found in 30–40% of follicular adult thyroid carcinoma, and rarely in FVPTC (11). The prevalence and type of mutations appear to differ between adult and childhood thyroid carcinoma, though pediatric data are still limited (1). Initial reports with relatively small sample sizes have shown a much lower prevalence of BRAF mutations in pediatric populations, ranging from 0% to 24% (12–14). In contrast, two recent reports demonstrated a much higher prevalence of the mutation in pediatric PTC of 34.5% and 71.4% (15,16). Sporadic pediatric thyroid cancer shows a variable prevalence of RET/PTC rearrangements, ranging from 37.5% to 71%, with RET/PTC1 being the predominant mutation (17–19). RAS mutations are uncommon in children and adolescents (20–22). The significance of these genetic mutations in terms of tumor presentation, progression, and response to therapeutic interventions in pediatrics is not clear. Therefore, this study investigated the rate of the common mutations implicated in non-medullary pediatric well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma (WDTC) in patients who underwent surgery at the authors' institution. This is the first pediatric study where all four mutation classes were examined on thyroidectomy-obtained thyroid tissue, and the findings were recently reported as an abstract (23). Correlations between genotype and clinical phenotype were also explored. The patients were identified based on ICD9 codes (193, 244.0, 244.1), and review of pathology records. Patients with medullary carcinoma were excluded. Forty-six consecutive children and adolescent patients with WDTC were identified between 2001 and 2013. Tumors of patients with only one tissue block available were not submitted for analysis. The protocol was IRB approved to analyze these blocks for commercially available BRAF, NRAS, HRAS, and KRAS point mutations, as well as RET/PTC and PAX8/PPARγ rearrangements, using validated molecular methods. The aim of this study was to describe the long-term oncological outcomes of pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) in a national cohort, and to identify risk factors for recurrence. Methods: We conducted a nationwide, retrospective cohort study, in which we combined two national databases. Patients aged <18 years, diagnosed with PTC or FTC in the Netherlands between 2000 and 2016, were included. pT-stage, pN-stage, multifocality and angioinvasion were included in a Cox-regression analysis for the identification of risk factors for recurrence. Results: 133 patients were included: 110 with PTC and 23 with FTC. Patients with PTC most often presented with pT2 tumors (24%) and pN1b (45%). During a median follow-up of 11.3 years, 21 patients with PTC developed a recurrence (19%). Nineteen recurrences were regional (91%) and 2 were pulmonary (9%). No risk factors for recurrence could be determined. One patient who developed pulmonary recurrence died two years later. Cause of death was not captured. Patients with FTC most often presented with pT2 tumors (57%). One patient presented with pN1b (4%). In 70%, no lymph nodes were collected. None of the patients with FTC developed a recurrence or died. Conclusion: Pediatric PTC and FTC are two distinct diseases. Recurrence in pediatric PTC is common, but in FTC it is not. Survival for both pediatric PTC and FTC is very good. Introduction Pediatric thyroid cancer is rare and represents only 2.3% of all thyroid cancer diagnoses (1). In children, 85% of the cases are papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and only 8% are follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) (2). Both types are a form of differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) (2). Pediatric PTC and pediatric FTC exhibit major clinical differences. Pediatric PTC is generally multifocal, bilateral and often presents with cervical lymph node metastases (3–5). Contrarily, pediatric FTC is generally unifocal and is more prone to hematogenous metastases, mainly to the lungs (3, 6). Cervical lymph node metastases are less common in children with FTC (6). In pediatric PTC, recurrence is very common, with rates ranging from 13% to 37% (4, 5, 7, 8). Conversely, long-term outcome data of pediatric FTC are very sparse. The limited data available suggest high survival rates and possibly lower to similar recurrence rates compared to pediatric PTC (6, 9). Nevertheless, most previous studies regarding pediatric thyroid cancer included only patients with PTC or reported on patients with DTC indiscriminately, as FTC is exceedingly rare. In addition, most studies included children and adolescents up to 21 years of age. Consequently, there is a lack of knowledge concerning the true long-term oncological outcomes of PTC and FTC, separately, in children younger than 18 years of age. Therefore, this study aimed to describe the long-term oncological outcomes of pediatric PTC and pediatric FTC in a national cohort, and to identify risk factors for recurrence. Methods This study was conducted as retrospective, nationwide, population-based cohort study and is reported according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines (10). This study has been approved by the institutional review board of Amsterdam UMC. Nationwide data of patients with differentiated thyroid carcinoma between 0 and 18 years of age, in the period from 2000 to 2016, were collected from the ‘Netherlands Cancer Registry’ (NCR). Recurrence data were collected by matching the cohort with data from the Nationwide Network and Registry of Histo- and Cytopathology in the Netherlands (PALGA) (11). Patients who did not match the PALGA-database were excluded, because there was no confirmation of pathology or recurrence data of these patients. Using the database of PALGA and in consultation with a pathologist, all patients were retrospectively reclassified in accordance with the staging criteria of the eighth edition of the TNM classification system (12). According to the Dutch National guidelines (13, 14), all children were treated in pediatric tertiary referral centers. Synchronous metastases were collected from the NCR-database. Cytology- or pathology proven metachronous metastases were collected from the PALGA-database. Branch report on molecular alterations by age in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma

The most common molecular alterations in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) are BRAFV600E, RET/PTC rearrangements, and NTRK fusions. In a large single-institution series of pediatric PTCs, BRAFV600E was the most frequent alteration, occurring in 36.8% of 163 cases, followed by NTRK3 fusion (11%), NRAS mutation (10.4%), and RET fusion (10.4%) [N1-F1]. A separate pediatric thyroid cancer cohort found BRAFV600E in 32.1% of PTC patients and RET/PTC in 21.4%, with RET/PTC occurring only in PTC and not in follicular variants [N2-F2]. This suggests that BRAF and RET/PTC are the dominant driver alterations in pediatric PTC, while NTRK fusions are also important but less frequent [N1-R4].

Age-related differences are evident in the frequency and association of these alterations. In the pediatric thyroid cancer cohort, BRAFV600E was strongly associated with older age: 89% of BRAFV600E mutations were found in adolescents >15 years of age, while only 11.1% were in patients ≤15 years old [N2-R1]. By contrast, RET/PTC rearrangements were more common in younger patients; the same cohort found all RET/PTC-positive patients were ≤15 years old [N2-R1]. In a pediatric PTC series, fusion-driven tumors showed more aggressive clinico-pathological features compared to mutation-driven and wild-type cases, with larger tumors, infiltrative growth, extrathyroidal extension, and N1b disease being more common in fusion-positive cases [N1-F1]. This indicates that age is not just a passive correlate but is linked to the molecular profile and the resulting tumor behavior.

The evidence also supports distinct subtypes or variants associated with specific alterations. Fusion-driven PTCs were enriched for solid growth patterns, and the study explicitly notes that solid growth is more frequently seen in gene-fusion cases [N1-F1]. In addition, the article states that PTCs showing solid growth pattern were significantly enriched in gene fusions [N1-F1], which aligns with the idea that molecular alterations can define subtypes. The review on thyroid cancer pathogenesis notes that thyroid cancer involves dysregulation of the MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, and that molecular techniques are typically applied to cytological smears [N5-R2][N5-R3]. This provides background context that molecular alterations are not merely random events but are central to the biology of PTC and are often grouped into pathway-based or fusion-based categories [N5-R2][N5-R3].

Taken together, the evidence suggests a molecular profile that changes with age within pediatric age groups: younger patients are more likely to have RET/PTC rearrangements and other fusion events, while older adolescents are more likely to have BRAFV600E mutations [N2-R1][N1-F1]. The alterations are also associated with distinct subtypes, particularly solid growth patterns and aggressive clinico-pathological features in fusion-driven tumors [N1-F1]. The broader thyroid cancer literature reinforces that molecular alterations are central to tumor biology and that BRAF, RET, and NTRK are key driver events [N5-R3][N5-R5].

The most relevant prognostic factors in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) include recurrence risk, staging features, and molecular alterations. A nationwide population-based study found that pediatric PTC recurrence is very common, with recurrence rates ranging from 13% to 37% across studies [N4-R1]. In that cohort, 19% of 110 pediatric PTC patients developed recurrence after a median follow-up of 11.3 years, with 91% of recurrences regional and 9% distant [N4-F4]. A separate study reported that recurrence was especially common in younger children, with younger vs older children showing more advanced disease at diagnosis, and that recurrence rates in pediatric PTC are high overall [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This suggests that recurrence is a central prognostic issue, with substantial variability in how often it occurs.

Age itself affects recurrence and long-term survival. The same nationwide study found that younger children had more advanced disease at presentation and that survival was excellent overall, but it also noted that recurrence was common [N4-R4][N4-R5]. Another cohort study reported that pediatric thyroid cancer usually presents at an advanced stage, carries an excellent prognosis, and has 10-year survival rates greater than 98% [N4-R3]. A separate study found excellent survival in younger children compared to adolescents and older children, but again emphasized that papillary thyroid cancer is more advanced at diagnosis in younger vs older children [N4-R4]. This indicates that age modifies both presentation and outcome: younger children tend to present more advanced disease, yet long-term survival remains favorable, while recurrence remains high.

Molecular alterations may modify prognosis or treatment response, though the evidence is mixed and primarily indirect. The pediatric PTC cohort found that fusion-driven tumors showed more aggressive clinico-pathological features compared to mutation-driven and wild-type cases, with larger tumors, infiltrative growth, extrathyroidal extension, and N1b disease being more common in fusion-positive cases [N1-F1]. This suggests that molecular alteration type can influence prognosis. In addition, the article notes that fusion-driven tumors are more likely to be associated with aggressive features and that testing for gene fusions is emerging as essential for routine molecular pathology [N1-F1]. The broader thyroid cancer literature also states that kinase fusions are associated with more invasive features in pediatric PTC, while BRAF mutations predict worse prognosis in adult PTC [N2-R2]. Although the evidence does not directly show that molecular alterations change response to treatment, it does indicate that molecular classification is increasingly important for clinical decision-making and that targeted therapies may become relevant as rearranged genes are identified [N1-F1][N2-R2].

Overall, the strongest prognostic factors are recurrence risk, staging features, and molecular alterations. Age affects disease presentation and recurrence, while molecular alterations are associated with more aggressive features and may influence treatment strategy [N4-R1][N4-F4][N4-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence supports a model in which molecular profiling is becoming integral to prognosis and clinical management, but the available data remain somewhat heterogeneous across age groups and settings [N1-F1][N2-R2].

Clinical presentation of pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is largely asymptomatic, often manifesting as a painless neck mass. The evidence states that pediatric thyroid cancers typically present as neck masses with no associated symptoms and come to medical attention at widely varying stages of disease [N3-R1]. The Cleveland Clinic notes that the main sign of PTC is a painless lump or nodule on the thyroid gland, and that PTC usually does not cause other symptoms [N3-R2]. Medscape similarly reports that thyroid carcinoma in pediatric patients usually manifests as an asymptomatic neck mass and that a painless noninflammatory metastatic cervical mass is also typical [N3-R4]. This suggests that presentation is generally non-specific and often late, with the dominant feature being a neck mass rather than symptoms such as pain, weight loss, or dysphagia.

Age appears to correlate with tumor size, location, and associated features. The 2024 New York-Presbyterian report explicitly states that pediatric PTC typically presents as a solitary nodule, tends to grow slowly, and often spreads to the lymph nodes in the neck [N3-F3]. It also reports that at diagnosis, up to 40–60% of children with PTC will have thyroid cancer that has spread to the lymph nodes in the neck, and approximately 10–15% of patients with lymph node metastases will have thyroid cancer that has spread to the lungs [N3-F3]. This indicates that lymph node involvement is common, and that the disease may extend beyond the thyroid early in the course. The evidence also suggests that younger children may present with more advanced disease: the study notes that prepubertal children are more likely to have more advanced disease at diagnosis than adolescents or young adults [N3-F3]. In addition, the abstract from the pediatric thyroid cancer cohort found that BRAFV600E was most common in older patients, while RET/PTC was more common in younger patients [N2-R1], which indirectly supports age-related differences in tumor biology and presentation.

Age may also affect diagnostic workup and staging approach. The article emphasizes that pediatric PTC is highly treatable, but optimal management is age-dependent, and that treatment typically consists of total thyroidectomy and surgical resection of involved lymph nodes [N3-F3]. It also notes that there are many open questions regarding the optimal management of PTC in young versus older children, and that the American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines for pediatric PTC were published to address these uncertainties [N3-F3]. The staging evidence in the same source indicates that pediatric PTC often presents with advanced disease, and that staging approaches must account for this [N3-F3]. While the provided evidence does not give a detailed staging table, it clearly supports the idea that pediatric PTC is staged using the same general principles as adult disease, but with age-related differences in how often aggressive features such as lymph node metastasis and extrathyroidal extension are present [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore suggests that age modifies the interpretation of staging because younger children are more likely to present with advanced disease, even though overall survival remains excellent [N3-F3][N4-R3].

Incidence and presentation vary by pediatric age group, but the evidence is somewhat indirect and heterogeneous. The ThyCa statistics note that papillary and follicular thyroid cancer account for only approximately 1% of all pediatric cancers in the 5–9 year old age group and up to 7% in adolescent cancer cases [N2-R3]. The 2024 New York-Presbyterian article also reports that pediatric PTC is the most common form of differentiated thyroid carcinoma in children, with pediatric DTC accounting for 1% of all pediatric cancer cases in prepubertal children and rising to 7% in adolescent cancer cases [N3-F3]. This indicates that incidence increases with age within the pediatric spectrum. The article also notes that incidence is slowly rising, which may affect how age groups are sampled in studies [N3-F3]. The provided evidence does not give a precise age-specific incidence curve, but it does establish that younger children and adolescents are not equivalent epidemiologically and that incidence is higher in older adolescents [N2-R3][N3-F3].

Presentation also varies by age group. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that pediatric PTC typically presents as a solitary nodule and that up to 40–60% of children with PTC will have lymph node metastasis at diagnosis, with approximately 10–15% of those with lymph node metastases also having lung metastasis [N3-F3]. The New York-Presbyterian article explicitly states that prepubertal children are more likely to have more advanced disease at diagnosis than adolescents or young adults [N3-F3]. This suggests that younger children are more likely to present with more aggressive features, even though the disease is often asymptomatic and presents as a neck mass [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The age-related difference in BRAFV600E and RET/PTC prevalence also supports this pattern: BRAFV600E is more common in older patients, while RET/PTC is more common in younger patients [N2-R1]. Together, these findings indicate that incidence and presentation are both age-related, with older adolescents tending to have BRAFV600E-driven tumors and younger children tending to have more advanced disease [N2-R3][N2-R1][N3-F3].

Staging approaches in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma are generally based on the standard TNM system, but the evidence suggests that age can modify interpretation. The New York-Presbyterian article states that pediatric PTC is highly treatable and that optimal management is age-dependent, with treatment typically consisting of total thyroidectomy and surgical resection of involved lymph nodes [N3-F3]. It also notes that staging approaches must be tailored to pediatric patients because younger children often present with more advanced disease [N3-F3]. The broader evidence on thyroid cancer staging indicates that the American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines for pediatric PTC were developed precisely because the relationship between age and tumor aggressiveness was unclear [N3-F3]. Therefore, age modifies the interpretation of staging and residual disease because younger children are more likely to present with advanced features such as lymph node metastasis and extrathyroidal extension, which may change management decisions even if overall survival remains excellent [N3-F3][N4-R3]. The evidence does not provide a detailed staging algorithm, but it clearly supports the need for age-stratified interpretation in staging and treatment planning.

## Integrated final answer on molecular alterations in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma across age

Pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is defined by a distinctive molecular landscape that changes with age, and these molecular alterations have important consequences for clinical presentation and prognosis. The evidence from the branch reports shows that younger children and adolescents differ in the frequency and biological consequences of driver alterations, and that these differences are linked to tumor behavior, staging, and treatment considerations.

### 1) Molecular alterations most common in pediatric papillary thyroid carcinoma

The most common molecular alterations in pediatric PTC are **BRAFV600E**, **RET/PTC rearrangements**, and **NTRK fusions**. In a large single-institution series of pediatric PTCs, **BRAFV600E** was the most frequent alteration, found in **36.8%** of 163 cases, followed by **NTRK3 fusion** (11%), **NRAS mutation** (10.4%), and **RET fusion** (10.4%) [N1-F1]. A separate pediatric thyroid cancer cohort found **BRAFV600E** in **32.1%** of PTC patients and **RET/PTC** in **21.4%**, with **RET/PTC** occurring only in PTC and not in follicular variants [N2-F2].
